title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Imagine that Hospital A has a higher survival rate than Hospital B for both mild and severe cases. It seems obvious that Hospital A must also have a higher survival rate overall.
Surprisingly, that conclusion can be wrong.
This phenomenon is called Simpson’s paradox: a relationship that appears within multiple groups can disappear or reverse when the groups are combined. It feels unintuitive because we expect an overall average to preserve a pattern found in every subgroup. However, an average depends not only on the outcomes within each group, but also on how heavily each group is represented.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
A Hospital Example
Consider the following hypothetical data:








Patient group
Hospital A
Hospital B




Mild cases
90 of 100 survive (90%)
760 of 900 survive (84.4%)


Severe cases
300 of 900 survive (33.3%)
30 of 100 survive (30%)


All cases
390 of 1,000 survive (39%)
790 of 1,000 survive (79%)



Hospital A has the higher survival rate within both groups. Nevertheless, Hospital B has a much higher overall survival rate.
The following graph makes the reversal visible:





Survival rates by patient group and hospital. Source: hypothetical data constructed for this example.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
section: Where Does the Reversal Come From?
text:
Where Does the Reversal Come From?
There is no mathematical contradiction. Hospital A treats mostly severe cases, while Hospital B treats mostly mild cases. Because severe cases are less likely to survive regardless of the hospital, Hospital A’s overall rate is pulled downward.
An overall survival rate is a weighted average:
roverall=wmildrmild+wseverersevere.
r_{\text{overall}}
=
w_{\text{mild}} r_{\text{mild}}
+
w_{\text{severe}} r_{\text{severe}}.

Here, rr represents a survival rate and ww represents a group’s share of the hospital’s patients. The two weights sum to one.
For example, Hospital A’s mild-case weight is 100 / 1,000 = 0.10. The weights describe patient shares, not survival probabilities. Rates in the equations are proportions: 0.90 means 90%.
For Hospital A:
rA=0.10×90100+0.90×300900=0.39=39%.
r_A
=
0.10\times\frac{90}{100}
+
0.90\times\frac{300}{900}
=
0.39=39\%.

For Hospital B:
rB=0.90×760900+0.10×30100=0.79=79%.
r_B
=
0.90\times\frac{760}{900}
+
0.10\times\frac{30}{100}
=
0.79=79\%.

The two overall rates use very different weights. Hospital A’s average is dominated by severe cases, whereas Hospital B’s average is dominated by mild cases. The aggregate comparison therefore mixes together two separate questions: how successfully each hospital treats a given type of patient, and what types of patients each hospital receives.
To see what the weights change, imagine giving both hospitals the same hypothetical mix: half mild cases and half severe cases. Applying these common weights to the exact subgroup rates gives 61.7% for A and 57.2% for B. A is ahead again. These are standardized comparisons, not observed overall rates or a prediction about moving patients between hospitals. The reversal comes from changing the mix, not from an arithmetic mistake.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
section: Why Economists and Data Scientists Should Care
text:
Why Economists and Data Scientists Should Care
Simpson’s paradox illustrates the importance of confounding variables. A confounding variable can influence both the treatment or group being compared and the outcome being studied. In this example, illness severity differs across hospitals and is related to the probability of survival. Ignoring severity can therefore produce a misleading comparison of hospital performance.
Similar reversals can occur in economics. A region’s average wage can rise even if wages fall within every occupation, provided that employment shifts toward higher-paying occupations. A university can have a lower overall admission rate while having higher admission rates within individual departments. An investment strategy may appear successful in aggregate only because it was used more often during favorable market conditions.
However, the lesson is not simply to divide data into as many groups as possible. Whether we should control for a variable depends on the question and the causal relationships among variables. If illness severity existed before hospital selection and influenced both selection and survival, adjusting for it may create a fairer comparison. Even then, other differences between patients could remain. Controlling for a variable caused by the treatment itself, however, could hide part of the treatment’s total effect.

title: When Every Group Wins but the Average Loses: Simpson’s Paradox
text:
The Main Lesson
Whenever an average is presented, we should ask:
An average of what, and with what weights?
Aggregated statistics are not necessarily incorrect, but they may answer a different question from the one we care about. Simpson’s paradox reminds us that data do not interpret themselves. Good analysis requires understanding how the data were generated, identifying relevant subgroups, and deciding which comparisons are meaningful.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
text:
Two NHL teams scored 235 goals each, yet one won 48 games and the other only 28. In the records labeled 2006, the Minnesota Wild and Washington Capitals looked identical on scoring totals. Their results were far apart.
The difference becomes easier to understand when goals allowed enter the picture. The Minnesota Wild conceded 191 goals; the Washington Capitals conceded 286. That comparison raises a practical question: when reviewing a team’s season, how much do we miss by looking at offense alone?
I scraped 582 team-season records from Scrape This Site’s hockey pages. In this sample, goal differential—goals scored minus goals allowed—has a much stronger relationship with winning percentage than scoring alone.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
College-educated workers earned about 75.5% more per hour than high-school graduates in May 2024, based on the weighted medians in this sample. That is a large advantage. But whether it has grown since 2003 depends on which workers we compare: the gap increased slightly in the main sample and declined slightly when I restricted it to full-time workers.
That distinction matters when discussing education and pay. A large wage advantage today does not automatically mean the advantage is growing, or that graduates’ purchasing power has improved. The three figures separate real wage levels, the premium under different working-hours definitions, and the contrasting endpoint changes for men and women.
I use IPUMS Current Population Survey data for employed wage and salary workers aged 25–54, comparing May observations from 2003 through 2024. These are historical snapshots, not a measure of today’s job market.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
text:
Eating out got more expensive faster than buying groceries over the decade from January 2015 to December 2024. U.S. prices for food away from home rose 48.1%, compared with 26.8% for food at home. Yet groceries experienced the higher peak in annual inflation.
Those findings answer two different questions: how much have prices risen, and when were they rising fastest? The distinction matters for anyone trying to understand why food still feels expensive after inflation slows.
I compare monthly food price indexes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, retrieved through FRED. These are national urban averages for a fixed historical period, not today’s menu or supermarket prices.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
text:
Eating out pulled further ahead








Figure 1: Both series start at January 2015 = 100. The lines compare price changes, not the dollar cost of equivalent meals.





Both lines begin at 100 in January 2015, making their percentage changes comparable. By December 2024, the cumulative increase for eating out exceeded that for groceries by 21.2 percentage points.
The gap was already developing before the pandemic. Grocery prices stayed relatively close to their starting level for several years, while food-away-from-home prices kept rising. Looking only at the later grocery surge would miss that earlier divergence.
For me, the useful distinction is between a smaller price increase and a cheaper meal. This chart establishes the first, not the second. It cannot tell us how many dollars someone saves by cooking the same dinner at home. That would require actual meal prices, and a broader comparison would include cooking time.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
section: Groceries had the sharper inflation peak
text:
Groceries had the sharper inflation peak








Figure 2: Year-over-year inflation compares each month with the same month one year earlier. A falling positive rate means prices are still increasing.





Grocery inflation peaked at 13.5% in August 2022, compared with a peak of 8.8% in March 2023 for eating out. Groceries had the more intense annual increase even though they rose less over the full decade.
That is why I would read these two charts together. The first shows the accumulated increase; the second reveals when the pressure intensified. Neither alone gives the full picture of how food prices changed.
By December 2024, annual inflation had slowed to 1.8% for groceries and 3.6% for eating out. This meant prices were above their levels a year earlier, but increasing more slowly than at the peaks. It did not undo the previous increases. Lower inflation and an expensive grocery bill can coexist.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
text:
Your shopping basket matters








Figure 3: Six major food-at-home categories, January 2015 to December 2024. These are category increases, not weighted contributions to total grocery inflation.





Even within groceries, the increases differed. Nonalcoholic beverages rose 30.9%, compared with 18.4% for fruits and vegetables. A single grocery average hides that variation.
For a household budget, I would look at frequently purchased categories as well as the headline index. Someone’s exposure depends on how much of their spending goes to each category. These bars do not measure any particular household’s inflation, and the largest percentage increase need not make the largest contribution to its bill.
A smaller increase also does not make a category cheaper in dollar terms. The chart gives a reason to examine the shopping basket, not a shopping list of what to substitute.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
text:
What the comparison tells us
Eating out had the larger cumulative increase, while groceries had the sharper inflation peak. The answer to “which rose faster?” depends on the time frame. For budgeting, I would pay attention to both accumulated increases and recent inflation, then compare them with what I actually buy.
These indexes cannot explain why prices changed or decide whether cooking is worth someone’s time. They do show why slowing inflation does not mean a return to earlier prices.

title: Eating Out vs. Eating In: Which Prices Rose Faster?
text:
Data, methods and reproducibility
I use eight monthly BLS CPI-U series: food at home, food away from home, and six grocery categories. All are U.S. city averages without seasonal adjustment. I set January 2015 = 100 for cumulative comparisons and calculate annual inflation against the same month a year earlier, using 2014 observations for the first year’s rates. The code checks monthly coverage, duplicates and invalid values. Results depend on the chosen endpoints and do not describe a specific store or student budget.
Sources: BLS CPI, FRED’s food at home and food away from home series. All eight source links are recorded in results/series_dictionary.csv.
The GitHub repository contains the R code and replication README. Original CSVs and retrieval records are saved in data/raw, charts in figures, and calculated tables and R session information in results. Later renders reuse the saved inputs.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
text:
Identical scoring totals, different seasons



Source: Scrape This Site; year label 2006









Team
Goals scored

Wins

Minnesota Wild
235

58.5%


Washington Capitals
235

34.1%





Minnesota’s goal differential was +44; Washington’s was -51. The winning percentages were 58.5% and 34.1%, respectively. A ranking based only on goals scored would treat them as equals, missing a substantial difference in their records.
I selected the same-year, equal-scoring pair with the largest winning-percentage gap in the sample. It is a deliberately clear illustration, not a typical pair or proof that goals allowed caused the entire difference. The broader comparison below uses all the records.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
section: Scoring matters, but leaves plenty unexplained
text:
Scoring matters, but leaves plenty unexplained








Figure 1: The same season’s total goals scored and reported winning percentage.





Goals scored and winning percentage have a correlation of 0.48. The upward pattern makes sense, but the spread matters too: similar scoring totals occur alongside quite different winning percentages. For a quick review, I would treat goals scored as one piece of information rather than a complete assessment of performance.
Correlation ranges from −1 to 1. A value closer to 1 indicates a stronger positive linear relationship—not the percentage of wins explained or evidence of causation.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
section: Adding goals allowed brings the pattern into focus
text:
Adding goals allowed brings the pattern into focus








Figure 2: Goal differential includes both scoring and goals allowed.





For goal differential, the correlation rises to 0.89. Teams that outscored their opponents more heavily generally won a larger share of games in this sample.
This is not a surprising new law of hockey: scoring and conceding are directly connected to game outcomes. The useful finding is how much tighter the relationship becomes when both sides enter the comparison. It supports using goal differential as a first summary of a completed season, then checking offense and goals allowed separately.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
section: What I would do with this comparison
text:
What I would do with this comparison
For a fan or analyst preparing a season review, I would use a two-step checklist: first compare teams’ goal differentials within the same season; then inspect goals scored and allowed separately to explain the ranking. The opening table shows what an offense-only comparison misses, the first scatterplot shows that problem across the sample, and the second shows how adding goals allowed tightens the relationship. The recommendation concerns describing completed seasons, not choosing next year’s players.
I would not use these correlations alone to predict next season or recommend a roster change. All measures describe the same completed seasons. The data pool different schedules and scoring environments, and total goals are not per-game rates. The teaching-site records have not been independently verified against official NHL statistics.
The takeaway is straightforward: before calling a team strong because it scores a lot, check what it gives up. That is a more useful way to read these results than treating the larger correlation as a forecasting model.

title: Same Goals, Different Results: What Scoring Misses in the NHL
text:
Data, methods and reproducibility
I used rvest to collect the first 24 pages of a public scraping practice site. This is a subset, not a claim to cover every available record. New requests are spaced one second apart; saved HTML pages are reused on later renders. No login, CAPTCHA or paywall is bypassed.
After numeric conversion and removal of 0 incomplete rows, the sample contains 582 team-seasons with year labels 1990–2011. I check duplicate team-year records and value ranges, retain the site’s reported winning percentage, and calculate Pearson correlations. Retrieval dates and source URLs are saved with the data.
To reproduce this post, start with the Post 2 README, then open index.qmd, the complete R analysis. Source snapshots and raw data are in data/raw, cleaned data in data/clean, charts in figures, and correlations and the example-selection results in results. The docs/ copy is generated website output, not the analysis entry point.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: A large advantage, little change at the endpoints
text:
A large advantage, little change at the endpoints








Figure 1: Weighted median real hourly earnings by education, May 2003–2024.





In May 2024, workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher had median hourly earnings of $38.00, compared with $21.65 for high-school graduates and $24.05 for those with some college or an associate degree.
The separation between the groups is clear. The change over time is less dramatic: in May 2024 dollars, the college median was $37.65 in 2003, while the high-school median was $21.98. Both were close to their 2024 levels.
I read this as a distinction between relative advantage and progress in purchasing power. College graduates can remain well ahead of another group without their own real median earnings rising much. Neither finding cancels the other.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: Is the gap growing? The comparison matters
text:
Is the gap growing? The comparison matters
The college wage premium measures how much higher the college median is than the high-school median, as a percentage of the high-school median.








Figure 2: College wage premiums in the main sample and among workers usually working at least 35 hours per week. Identical axes make both the size of the advantage and the differing endpoint changes visible. Labels mark May 2003 and May 2024; intermediate years are also shown.





The premium moved from 71.3% in 2003 to 75.5% in 2024, with fluctuations in between. It reached 84.5% in 2022 before falling. That is not a steady upward path.
The right panel restricts the sample to workers usually working at least 35 hours per week. Here, the premium moved from 71.9% to 70.4%. The endpoint direction reverses, although the large college advantage remains. The full series shows fluctuations, not a steady decline.
Together, the panels support a narrower conclusion: this sample shows a persistent education gap, but not a widening gap that is robust to including or excluding part-time workers. This is a comparison of sample definitions, not evidence that working full-time causes a smaller premium. I have not calculated confidence intervals, so the endpoint movements are not established statistically significant changes.
Employment composition also matters. A rise in the median can reflect changes in who is working, not just pay increases. These comparisons do not follow individual workers’ wage growth or establish what caused the movements around 2020.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: One overall number hides different patterns
text:
One overall number hides different patterns








Figure 3: Within-sex college wage premiums in May 2003 and May 2024.





Among women, the premium rose from 76.1% to 82.1%; among men, it fell from 71.5% to 66.7%. The overall comparison conceals these different directions.
A larger premium for women does not mean women earn more than men. Each percentage compares college and high-school graduates within the same sex. It also cannot tell us whether education itself explains the gap: occupation, experience and selection into employment may differ.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
section: What I take from these results
text:
What I take from these results
The three figures tell one economic story: a large education wage gap can persist without strong real wage growth or a uniform increase in the premium. Figure 1 shows college graduates remaining well ahead, even though the college and high-school real medians changed little between the endpoints. Figure 2 shows a modest endpoint increase in the main sample but a modest decrease among full-time workers. Figure 3 shows another contrast: the within-sex premium rose for women and fell for men between 2003 and 2024.
The takeaway is therefore not that the gap is simply growing or shrinking. It is that the college advantage remains large, while its measured change depends on working hours and the group being compared. Those differences belong in the explanation of education and inequality, rather than being hidden behind one overall number. The observed changes are descriptive, not statistically established trends.
These results also do not settle whether college is worth its cost. They describe employed workers, include graduate degrees, and do not measure tuition, forgone earnings or the causal effect of attending college.

title: The College Wage Premium: Large, but Not Steadily Growing
text:
Data, methods and reproducibility
The sample contains 171,391 person-month observations with at least a high-school qualification. I exclude self-employed workers and invalid earnings or hours. Hourly earnings are weekly earnings divided by usual main-job hours; all medians use EARNWT, the CPS earnings-study weight. BLS CPI-U converts wages to May 2024 dollars. These are May snapshots, not annual averages.
I use the harmonized rounded earnings series and cap weekly earnings at $2,884.61 across years. The cap leaves the overall education-group medians unchanged, but does not eliminate all measurement differences from the 2023–2024 reporting changes. Imputed earnings remain included because allocation flags were not downloaded.
Sources: IPUMS CPS, its earnings and weight documentation, and BLS CPI-U. The repository and README provide code, saved figures and results, plus instructions for obtaining the IPUMS extract and reproducing the analysis.

title: Does Cheaper Rent Mean More Affordable Housing?
text:
A lower monthly rent looks like a better deal. But a cheaper apartment can still take a larger share of a household’s income. Where in Philadelphia does lower rent actually mean a lighter burden for the people living there?
The answer is not a simple map of expensive and inexpensive areas. In the 2019–2023 American Community Survey (ACS), 58.8% of eligible renter households in the lowest-rent quarter of the tracts studied spent at least 30% of income on rent, compared with 41.0% in the highest-rent quarter. Lower prices did not necessarily mean less financial pressure.

title: Does Cheaper Rent Mean More Affordable Housing?
text:
Two maps, two different questions
The left map shows each census tract’s median monthly gross rent, which includes utilities. The right shows the share of renter households spending at least 30% of income on gross rent. I call this rent burden; households whose ratios cannot be computed are excluded from that denominator. Citywide, the estimated share was 52.0%.






Figure 1: Philadelphia census tracts, ACS 2019–2023. Colors show estimates, not precise neighborhood rankings. Gray tracts lack a usable median rent or have fewer than 100 estimated households with a computed rent-to-income ratio.



Around City Hall, many tracts have comparatively high rents but lighter burdens. Several areas to the north and west show the opposite combination: lower rents alongside larger shares of burdened renters. The pattern is uneven, with exceptions in both directions. Census tracts are statistical areas, not exact neighborhood boundaries.
That mismatch is the important geographic finding. A rent map describes the price of housing occupied by current residents. A burden map adds their ability to pay. An expensive area can look less strained because the households living there can afford more, while a lower-priced area can still leave residents stretched. These maps alone do not establish why households or housing prices differ across places.

title: Does Cheaper Rent Mean More Affordable Housing?
section: Comparing the same city more systematically
text:
Comparing the same city more systematically
To move beyond visually comparing colors, I sorted 376 tracts into four equal-sized groups by median rent. Within each group, I added the estimated burdened households and divided by all households with computed ratios. This gives households proportional influence rather than treating every tract’s percentage equally.






Figure 2: Groups are based on tract median rent, not individual households’ rents. Whiskers show approximate 90% intervals conditional on these estimated groups; they do not include uncertainty in group assignment.



The lowest-rent group had tract medians of $407–$1,125, yet its burden rate was about 17.8 percentage points higher than the highest-rent group’s. The direction remains when I require at least 200 or 300 eligible households per tract, and when I exclude tracts with particularly imprecise burden estimates. These checks support the broad comparison, not a ranking of individual blocks.
This does not mean a household would save money by moving to a more expensive area. The groups contain different households and housing. Nor does the comparison establish that higher rents cause lower burdens.

title: Does Cheaper Rent Mean More Affordable Housing?
section: What I would take from this
text:
What I would take from this
If I were using a map to identify housing pressure, I would look at rent burden alongside rent levels. Focusing only on the most expensive areas could overlook residents under substantial pressure in cheaper ones. A practical next step would be to examine high-burden areas’ housing conditions and eligibility for assistance before targeting resources.
There are limits. ACS five-year estimates pool 2019–2023 responses; they are not today’s advertised rents. Individual tract estimates can have wide sampling errors, and household size, subsidies, and housing quality are not controlled here. The analysis includes 376 of 408 tracts, covering about 99.2% of citywide households with computed ratios.
For me, the useful distinction is between cheaper housing and housing that residents can afford. A price map answers only the first question.

title: Does Cheaper Rent Mean More Affordable Housing?
text:
Sources and reproduction
I use Census ACS tables B25064 and B25070, downloaded from the official table-based Summary File, and 2023 Census cartographic boundaries. Dollar values are in 2023 dollars.
The Post 5 README links the R scripts, saved source data, calculated tables, and replication instructions. Rendering regenerates the maps, chart, and numerical statements above.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
text:
Would you judge a movie from its opening scene? This post asks a similar measurement question about income: how strongly do mothers’ earnings predict their children’s, and does the estimate change when we measure income later or over more years?
I use the University of Michigan’s PSID-SHELF, covering 42 survey waves from 1968 through 2021. This is a tutorial in measurement, not a claim that parents determine their children’s destinies.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
section: 1. Find the family—not just a similar surname
text:
1. Find the family—not just a similar surname
The extract contains 84,121 people, including years without observations. ID identifies a person; REL_PAR_BM_ID identifies their biological mother. Siblings share a mother, making this a many-to-one match. After the extraction step in the replication guide, open the private database:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
con = sqlite3.connect("private/selected_columns.sqlite")
SQL’s GROUP BY reduces repeated person-year records to one mother link per child. HAVING excludes inconsistent links:
con.executescript("""
CREATE TEMP TABLE links AS
SELECT ID, MIN(REL_PAR_BM_ID) AS mother_id
FROM person_year
GROUP BY ID
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT REL_PAR_BM_ID) = 1
   AND MIN(REL_PAR_BM_ID) > 0;
""")
SELECT chooses columns; MIN retrieves the sole consistent mother ID. An identified mother is not necessarily observed: we still need her earnings records. Run the Python blocks in order from the post folder, in one fresh session, after extracting the data.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
section: 2. Put both generations on comparable clocks
text:
2. Put both generations on comparable clocks
Income refers to the previous tax year, so measurement age equals survey year minus one minus birth year. I use individual labor earnings in 2024 dollars, not household income. These measures are available for reference persons and spouses; other adult household members are not automatically covered.
I exclude missing, negative, and standardized topcoded amounts, but retain valid zeros in averages. Both generations need at least three observed income years at ages 30–39. AVG constructs the measure; HAVING enforces coverage:
con.executescript("""
CREATE TEMP TABLE valid AS
SELECT ID, YEAR, YEAR-1-DEMO_BIRTH_YEAR AS age, EARN_TOT_RD AS income
FROM person_year
WHERE REFCOUPLE=1 AND EARN_TOT_ND>=0
  AND EARN_TOT_ND<9999999 AND EARN_TOT_RD>=0;
CREATE TEMP TABLE averages AS
SELECT ID, AVG(income) AS average_income, COUNT(*) AS n_years
FROM valid
WHERE age BETWEEN 30 AND 39
GROUP BY ID
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
CREATE TEMP TABLE singles AS
SELECT ID, income, ROW_NUMBER() OVER
  (PARTITION BY ID ORDER BY ABS(age-35), YEAR) AS rn
FROM valid WHERE age BETWEEN 30 AND 39;
""")
For single-year income I select the observation nearest age 35, breaking ties toward the earlier year, before requiring positive earnings. I do not search for a more convenient positive paycheck.
JOIN connects matching IDs. Joining each income table twice retrieves child and mother measures. Requiring positive single-year and average incomes fixes one common comparison sample:


Show the complete comparison-sample join

matched = pd.read_sql_query("""
SELECT l.ID, l.mother_id, c.average_income AS child_average,
       m.average_income AS mother_average, cs.income AS child_single,
       ms.income AS mother_single
FROM links l
JOIN averages c ON l.ID=c.ID
JOIN averages m ON l.mother_id=m.ID
JOIN singles cs ON l.ID=cs.ID AND cs.rn=1
JOIN singles ms ON l.mother_id=ms.ID AND ms.rn=1
WHERE c.average_income>0 AND m.average_income>0
  AND cs.income>0 AND ms.income>0
ORDER BY l.ID
""", con)
assert matched.ID.is_unique and len(matched) == 3094

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
section: 3. Estimate persistence, then lengthen the snapshot
text:
3. Estimate persistence, then lengthen the snapshot
The intergenerational elasticity is the slope in
log(Ychild)=α+βlog(Ymother)+ε.\log(Y_{child})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{mother})+\varepsilon.
A slope of 0.09 associates 10% higher maternal earnings with approximately 0.9% higher child earnings—not a 9% inherited share or a causal effect. The calculation is:
def slope(parent, child):
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(parent)), np.log(parent)])
    return np.linalg.lstsq(X, np.log(child), rcond=None)[0][1]

single = slope(matched.mother_single, matched.child_single)
average = slope(matched.mother_average, matched.child_average)
print(f"Single: {single:.3f}; average: {average:.3f}")
The full script also clusters uncertainty by mother because siblings are not independent.



Single-year versus multiyear earnings, using the same sample.


Among the same 3,094 children and 1,753 mothers, the estimate rises from 0.068 for single-year earnings to 0.090 for multiyear averages. Mothers contribute 8.35 years on average; children contribute 5.39. Averaging can dampen temporary fluctuations, although it does not guarantee a lifetime-income measure.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
section: 4. Replay the same children at different ages
text:
4. Replay the same children at different ages
Next I hold maternal average earnings fixed and compare child earnings nearest ages 22, 35, and 45, within windows 20–24, 30–39, and 40–49. All three estimates use exactly the same 1,608 children and 1,116 mothers. This is a separate sample from Figure 1, not a directly comparable fourth bar.



Maternal-income associations at three child ages.


The point estimate increases from 0.014 near 22 to 0.042 near 35 and 0.051 near 45. Figure 1 changes the length of the snapshot; Figure 2 changes its timing. Figure 3 asks whether either apparent change is precisely estimated.



Paired differences and their uncertainty.


However, every paired 95% confidence interval includes zero. The age-45-minus-age-22 difference is 0.036, with an interval of −0.001 to 0.074. These results suggest a pattern; they do not establish bias relative to an unobserved true lifetime elasticity.
To demonstrate how lifecycle bias can arise, consider an explicitly hypothetical model: maternal lifetime log earnings are measured perfectly, and the child’s lifetime log earnings have a slope of 0.4 on them. If early child log earnings reflect only half those lifetime differences, the observed early slope is 0.2. At a mature-age loading of one, it is 0.4. These are assumed values, not PSID estimates or an explanation established for this sample.
This example separates systematic age distortion from temporary noise. Averaging can reduce transitory measurement noise, but averaging only early ages would retain the assumed half-loading. Neither the model nor our empirical comparison identifies the true lifetime elasticity in these data.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
section: 5. The takeaway: match people precisely, measure status patiently
text:
5. The takeaway: match people precisely, measure status patiently
In this selected PSID sample, multiyear averages and later-age earnings produce higher IGE point estimates, but the paired confidence intervals include zero. Figures 1 and 2 show the numerical pattern; Figure 3 shows that the evidence is insufficient to establish differences in the underlying associations. These results do not prove lifecycle bias or stronger inherited advantage.
These are unweighted, selected-sample associations. Long follow-up requirements, attrition, positive-income restrictions, and reference-couple coverage limit generalization. The earnings construction also excludes farming income after 1993, creating a comparability limitation. Neither averaging nor a larger sample eliminates these issues.
Can one paycheck tell the family’s economic story? It provides a snapshot, not a lifetime portrait. Accurate family matching is the first step; income definitions, measurement ages, and uncertainty must also be part of the answer.

title: Can One Paycheck Tell Your Family’s Economic Story?
text:
Code and data access
The replication guide and complete analysis include the age comparison, clustered uncertainty, and fixed specification. Raw PSID microdata remain private and must be obtained from the provider; they are not redistributed here.

title: Is an Early Flight Worth the Alarm?
text:
The 6 a.m. flight costs you sleep. A later one may cost you time at the airport. Which scheduled departure hours had fewer disruptions in the records—and does the answer change with the airport, airline, or month?
I examine 360,771 domestic flight records scheduled to leave JFK, LaGuardia (LGA), or Newark (EWR) during 2025, from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. A full calendar year avoids treating one season as typical. These are reporting-carrier records, not all international flights or a forecast for your next trip. The economic trade-off is practical: departure time is one choice travelers can compare when reliability matters alongside fare and convenience.

title: Is an Early Flight Worth the Alarm?
section: 1. Read the clock you can actually book
text:
1. Read the clock you can actually book
I group flights by scheduled, not actual, local departure hour. A delayed morning flight should not become an afternoon observation. Following BTS, an arrival at least 15 minutes late counts as delayed. Cancellations and diversions are retained as distinct outcomes, not discarded as missing arrival times.
The default disruption rate combines arrival delay, cancellation, and diversion, divided by records with a classified outcome. Arrival-delay rates alone use reported, non-cancelled, non-diverted arrivals; cancellation rates use all scheduled records. One record has an unclassified outcome; it is excluded from the disruption and arrival-delay denominators. These measures answer different questions.
For all three airports together, the 06:00–08:59 window had a 15.6% disruption rate, versus 39.0% at 18:00–20:59: a difference of 23.4 percentage points. Those windows were chosen before inspecting the results, not selected as the best and worst hours.


Explore the record, not just the average. Start with all airports, then select an airport, reporting airline, and month. Switch the outcome to distinguish arrival delay from cancellation. Hover or tap for counts; click a calendar cell to select its month. Use Reset to return to the full year.

View 1. How does the hourly rate change?

Source: BTS Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance, 2025; author’s calculations. Flight-weighted rates, not averages of airline percentages. Blank hours have fewer than 100 eligible records.
2. Is the annual pattern also the monthly pattern?
The calendar uses the same selected outcome and airport/airline filters, but always shows all 12 months. For the pooled full-year selection, July had the highest monthly disruption rate (37.3%), while September had the lowest (18.6%). These are whole-month rates, not the individual heatmap-cell rates. Darker cells indicate higher rates, not more flights. The fixed 0–100% color scale allows comparisons across selections.


Source: BTS, 2025; author’s calculations. Grey or blank cells are unavailable or below the 100-eligible-record threshold, never assumed to have zero delays.
3. Does the flight arrive late—or not arrive as planned?
A delay rate among completed flights leaves cancellations out. Across the full dataset, 2.6% of records were cancelled and 0.3% were diverted. The stacked view restores those outcomes to the denominator: all scheduled records in each hour band, for the chosen airport, airline, and month.

Source: BTS, 2025; author’s calculations. Arrival <15 minutes late includes early arrivals. All five categories sum to 100%; hour bands with fewer than 100 scheduled records are blank. Changing the outcome selector does not change this five-category breakdown.

JavaScript is required for the interactive charts. The downloadable counts and static preview are available in the repository.

title: Is an Early Flight Worth the Alarm?
section: 4. Check that the story is not just different routes
text:
4. Check that the story is not just different routes
The interactive views hold your selected airport and reporting airline fixed, but their routes can still differ across hours. As a separate check, I compare morning and evening within the same origin, destination, reporting airline, and month, requiring at least 30 classified outcomes in each window. Both windows receive identical pooled-cell weights.
The check retains 620 comparable groups covering 58,974 classified outcomes:

The common-group check preserves the direction of the pooled morning advantage, although its magnitude changes. Its retained records represent only 16.3% of all classified outcomes in the annual dataset; routes without enough records in both windows are excluded, so this check cannot represent every route. It is not a randomized comparison: flight schedules, passenger choices, weather, and other conditions are not held constant. The data do not identify why the pattern occurs.

title: Is an Early Flight Worth the Alarm?
section: Takeaway: check the pattern behind the average
text:
Takeaway: check the pattern behind the average
In these 2025 records, the morning comparison window had fewer recorded disruptions than the evening window. The hourly view shows the overall timing pattern; the calendar reveals how it varies by month; the outcome breakdown shows whether delay, cancellation, or diversion accounts for the recorded disruption share. No single pooled percentage supplies all three answers.
For a traveler, the useful step is to compare the available time windows for the relevant airport, airline, and season, rather than rely on a universal “best departure time.” These historical flight-level rates are not passenger-weighted probabilities or a causal benefit from changing your ticket. They exclude fares and missed-connection costs, so this is not a calculation of the cheapest or most valuable flight.
These are descriptive rates without confidence intervals or significance tests. The 100-record plotting threshold limits sparse displays; it does not establish statistical significance or justify precise rankings of neighboring hours. The results do not quantify uncertainty about future flights.

title: Is an Early Flight Worth the Alarm?
text:
Data and reproducibility
The replication guide identifies the cached NYC subset, original monthly downloads, definitions, and commands. Python computes additive counts; Plotly renders the interactive views locally without a server or CDN. Sparse hourly groups are hidden rather than presented as precise rankings. See BTS definitions and the complete analysis.

title: Was Your Delivery Slow—or Was Your Sample Unlucky?
text: Dinner took forever. Your last few orders felt slow, too. How much can a handful of deliveries tell you about average waiting time? The answer requires separating individual experiences, uncertainty about a mean, and evidence against a benchmark.

title: Was Your Delivery Slow—or Was Your Sample Unlucky?
text:
1. Real orders, uneven waits
Meituan is a Chinese food-delivery platform, comparable to DoorDash or Uber Eats. I use its official INFORMS TSL research dataset, retaining 546,364 completed, non-prebook orders dated October 17–24, 2022. Waiting time is delivery arrival minus order creation, in minutes—not just the courier’s travel time. Rejected assignment attempts are not separate completed orders; zero timestamps mean unavailable.
The retained reference set averages 29.65 minutes, with a median of 27.90. Yet 10.9% exceed 45 minutes. An average near half an hour can coexist with many frustrating waits.
I retain 81 waits over 120 minutes, including a maximum of 645.42 minutes. These extreme timestamps cannot be independently validated. Excluding waits over 120 minutes changes the mean to 29.62 minutes, a small change; the main analysis keeps them.



Distribution of real order-to-arrival times. The final bar pools all waits of 120 minutes or longer; no long waits are removed. Source: Meituan; author’s calculations.


For the experiments, treat these recorded durations as a fixed empirical population, drawing independently with replacement. We pretend the analyst sees only a small sample; the full reference set supplies the known mean for checking coverage, not for constructing that sample’s interval or test. The observations are real; the repeated samples are simulated.

title: Was Your Delivery Slow—or Was Your Sample Unlucky?
text:
2. One sample, many possible averages
The default example uses a fixed-seed sample of 100 orders and a 95% confidence level. Its mean is 29.86 minutes. Resample those same 100 observations with replacement 1,999 times, always keeping sample size 100, and calculate each resample’s mean. These are not new orders: the bootstrap approximates sampling uncertainty using the observed sample.
The middle 95% of bootstrap means gives a percentile interval of 27.59–32.24 minutes. Switch the controls to compare settings: chart summaries update, while prose examples retain their stated settings.


Sample size (all three interactive views)20 deliveries100 deliveries400 deliveries
Two-sided interval confidence (first two views)90%95%99%
Reset to n = 100, 95%

Change sample size to compare nested, fixed-seed samples. Change confidence to see the width–coverage trade-off. These are precomputed, reproducible experiments, not fresh simulations each time you click. Hover or tap for details.


Figure 2. Green bars: resampled means; green boundaries and shading: selected interval; dotted blue line: original sample mean. Source: author’s resampling of real Meituan deliveries.

3. Does “95%” actually work 95% of the time?
Now draw 1,000 new samples from the full reference distribution. For each, restart the bootstrap and construct a new interval. Because we know the reference mean, we can count successes. At n = 100, the 95% procedure covers it in 95.5% of experiments; at n = 20 and 400, coverage is 92.8% and 95.0%. Small samples need not achieve the label’s promise.


Figure 3. Green intervals cover the fixed reference mean; orange ones miss. Dashed blue line: reference mean. More Monte Carlo repetitions stabilize the estimated coverage; they do not repair a poorly calibrated interval. The first 60 experiments are displayed without selection.
The 95% describes repeated use of the procedure, not a 95% probability assigned to the fixed mean after seeing one interval. Nor is it a range containing 95% of individual delivery times. A narrower interval from a larger sample does not make your next dinner arrive more predictably.

4. Is there evidence that the mean exceeds 30 minutes?
Use a one-sided test: H₀: μ = 30 versus H₁: μ > 30. Thirty minutes is an illustrative benchmark, not a platform guarantee. Subtract the sample mean from each sampled duration and add 30, imposing the null before resampling. Generate 9,999 null samples and calculate T = sample mean − 30. This sample-centered bootstrap test approximates the null distribution; it is not an exact test for every possible delivery-time distribution.


Figure 4. Green line: observed statistic. Dashed orange line: approximate 95th percentile of the null distribution; the right tail is the 5% rejection region. Bin coloring approximates that boundary; p is calculated from individual simulated statistics, not histogram bars. Source: sample-centered empirical-null simulation. The test stays at α = 0.05 when interval confidence changes.
The p-value counts null statistics at least as large as observed, using (extreme count + 1)/(9,999 + 1). For the default 100-order sample, p = 0.5452, so do not reject the 30-minute null. This is not the probability that H₀ is true, and failing to reject does not prove equality. The one-sided test and two-sided interval are different procedures.

Enable JavaScript for interactive views. Static versions appear below.

title: Was Your Delivery Slow—or Was Your Sample Unlucky?
section: Takeaway: a slow dinner is not a statistical verdict
text:
Takeaway: a slow dinner is not a statistical verdict
More representative observations—not more resamples of the same few orders—provide more information about the service. The first figure shows why individual waits vary. The bootstrap quantifies uncertainty from one sample; repeated sampling checks its coverage; the null simulation asks whether an observed mean is unusually high under a stated benchmark.
As an illustration, the default 100-order sample gives a 95% interval of 27.59–32.24 minutes, and the one-sided test provides insufficient evidence that the mean exceeds 30 minutes. This is an example of interpreting uncertainty, not a verdict on the platform.
Real orders can share couriers, merchants and demand conditions. The independent-draw experiment deliberately removes that dependence; its coverage is not a guarantee for convenience samples or correlated customer histories. The data describe this historical release, not all customers. Without a comparison across periods, they cannot establish whether service has become slower or why.

title: Was Your Delivery Slow—or Was Your Sample Unlucky?
text:
Sources and reproducibility
This research was supported by data provided by Meituan. To respect the publisher’s redistribution restrictions, raw order records are not included in this repository. The replication guide provides the official download link and code to obtain the exact data version used, plus cleaning rules, seeds and saved outputs. Methods: percentile bootstrap documentation and Hesterberg’s discussion of bootstrap accuracy.
